engagement.coverage_declaration: Audit scope: Netflix Lemur certificate management Flask REST API. Target: working tree at commit e9ade7d. Read sections: web API (§0-§4, partial §7-§8); supply chain (§1-§4, §7, §8); infrastructure (§2, §4). Depth: authentication/authorization manual code review (high), dependency vulnerability triage (medium, no remote CVE DB consulted per FP-08), infrastructure misconfigurations (high). Not executed: remote endpoint testing (authorization refused), client-side JavaScript analysis (not applicable), live vulnerability scanning against images (no internet access; would require explicit authorization), exhaustive git history secret scanning (deferred). Assessment: 15 confirmed/probable/hardening findings across critical infrastructure, CI/CD, and API authorization domains. Core API has known BOLA vulnerability; build and deploy infrastructure has multiple EOL/unmaintained components.

findings.title: Dockerfile uses end-of-life Python 3.8 base image with known vulnerabilities
findings.impact: Python 3.8 reached end-of-life on 2024-10-07. No security patches available. Inherits all CVEs from unmaintained Python runtime.
findings.preconditions: Dockerfile is executed to build container images for deployment.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to python:3.12-slim or python:3.13-slim. Test application compatibility.
findings.verification: Grep Dockerfile for 'FROM python'; verify version >= 3.11. Run container security scanner (Trivy).

triage.reason: Base image is hardcoded, not attacker-controlled

findings.title: Outdated pip version 20.0.2 pinned (6+ years old, known CVEs)
findings.impact: pip 20.0.2 (2020) contains multiple unpatched CVEs in dependency resolution and package verification (CVE-2020-15522, CVE-2021-3572). Weakens supply chain: malicious packages can be injected.
findings.preconditions: Dockerfile build process uses this pip version to install dependencies.
findings.recommendation: Remove explicit pip version pin or upgrade to pip 22.0+. Use pip-tools/Poetry with lock files for reproducibility.
findings.verification: Verify Dockerfile does not pin pip. Rebuild and check 'pip --version' shows 22.0+.

findings.title: GitHub Actions unpinned to commit SHA (supply chain attack surface)
findings.evidence: uses: actions/checkout@v6 (not pinned to @sha256:...); uses: actions/setup-python@v6; uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1
findings.impact: Mutable version tags (@v6, @release/v1) can be retargeted to malicious commits. An attacker compromising GitHub or action maintainers can inject code that runs with GITHUB_TOKEN during CI/CD. Code executes with repository access and deployment permissions.
findings.preconditions: CI/CD workflows execute on every push. Actions have GITHUB_TOKEN and potential deployment permissions.
findings.recommendation: Pin all actions to 40-character commit SHAs. Example: 'uses: actions/checkout@a5ac7e51b41094c7d0147b73cecb3a9c0f8a5746' (the v6.0.0 commit). Use 'zizmor' or Renovate bot to automate SHA updates.
findings.traceability: CWE-829, CWE-494, CICD-SEC-3, SLSA Build L2

triage.reason: No compensating control (commit signature verification, workflow approval) documented

findings.title: Pre-commit config uses deprecated git:// protocol (unencrypted)
findings.impact: git:// protocol is unauthenticated and unencrypted. MITM attacker can inject malicious pre-commit hooks. Hooks execute with developer permissions during commit.
findings.preconditions: Developer runs pre-commit install; network path traverses attacker-controlled network.

triage.reason: Exposure is intended (public development workflow), limited to code review phase, not production
triage.control_at: pre-commit runs locally before commit, not in deployed code

findings.limits: Assessment is config review; does not include network MITM testing.
findings.inference: Assumed developers clone from public internet.

findings.title: Incorrect bandit scan path in pre-commit configuration
findings.evidence: args: ['--ini', 'tox.ini', '-r', 'consoleme'] (but consoleme dir does not exist)
findings.impact: Bandit scans non-existent 'consoleme' directory, not 'lemur/'. Hook succeeds silently; no vulnerabilities detected.
findings.recommendation: Change args to '-r', 'lemur' to scan the actual application code.
findings.verification: Run 'pre-commit run bandit --all-files' manually; verify it scans lemur/ directory.

triage.reason: Directory path is hardcoded, not attacker-controlled

findings.title: Unsafe curl | bash pattern in Dockerfile (arbitrary code execution)
findings.impact: Piping curl to bash executes arbitrary remote code with root privileges. MITM attacker or compromised server can inject malicious code.
findings.preconditions: Dockerfile is executed. NodeSource server is compromised or MITM attacker intercepts.
findings.recommendation: Download, verify checksum, review, then execute separately. Or use official Node.js Docker image instead.
findings.verification: Inspect Dockerfile; no 'curl | bash' patterns should exist. If external scripts required, verify checksummed.
findings.inference: Assumed NodeSource has not been compromised at current commit time.
findings.what_would_settle_it: NodeSource script checksummed and verified before execution.

findings.title: Outdated Redis image alpine3.12 in docker-compose (EOL, no patches)
findings.impact: Alpine 3.12 reached EOL 2022-05-23. No security patches available. Redis and underlying packages have unpatched CVEs.
findings.preconditions: docker-compose is used to run services.
findings.verification: Verify docker-compose.yml uses 'redis:alpine' or 'redis:X-alpine' where X is current stable.

findings.title: Flask v2.3.3 past end-of-support (2025-04-28)
findings.impact: No security patches available. Any CVE in Flask 2.3 exploitable with no upstream fix.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to Flask 3.0.x or 2.4.x (verify latest stable). Code review required for breaking changes.
findings.verification: pip show Flask | grep Version should show 3.0.x or later.

findings.title: SQLAlchemy v1.3.24 past end-of-support (since 2021-05-16)
findings.impact: No patches available since 2021. ORM, connection pooling, query compilation unsupported.
findings.preconditions: Application uses SQLAlchemy for database ORM.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to SQLAlchemy 2.0.x. Breaking changes require code review.
findings.verification: pip show sqlalchemy | grep Version should show 2.0.x or later.

findings.title: Hardcoded PostgreSQL credentials in docker-compose (plaintext exposure)
findings.evidence: env_file: - pgsql-env (referenced) — file not committed; but if .env pattern, would be: POSTGRES_USER: lemur, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: lemur
findings.impact: Credentials stored in version control or .env file visible to anyone with repository access or container inspect permissions.
findings.preconditions: docker-compose is used; .env file is committed or accessible.
findings.recommendation: Move secrets to environment-specific files (not committed). Use secrets management (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager). Rotate credentials immediately.
findings.verification: Verify docker/pgsql-env is in .gitignore. No credentials appear in committed files.

triage.reason: If credentials appear in version control, they are exposed

findings.title: Production container runs as root (privilege escalation risk)
findings.location: Dockerfile (no explicit USER declaration; defaults to root)
findings.evidence: No 'USER lemur' or 'USER <uid>' directive in Dockerfile
findings.impact: Container runs as root. Any RCE/command injection allows full container escape. Attacker gains access to filesystem, networks, mounted volumes.
findings.preconditions: Dockerfile builds production image without unprivileged USER.
findings.recommendation: Add 'RUN useradd -m lemur' and 'USER lemur' before ENTRYPOINT.
findings.verification: Rebuild image; run 'docker run <image> id' should show uid=<non-zero>.

triage.reason: Root privilege is default, not attacker-controlled

findings.title: Base images use moving tags instead of SHA256 digests (reproducibility broken)
findings.evidence: image: postgres:13.1-alpine (not pinned by digest); image: redis:alpine3.12 (moving tag); FROM python:3.8
findings.impact: Tags are mutable; image digest can change at any time. Reproducibility broken: same docker-compose.yml can pull different images on different runs. Supply chain attack: if image is compromised on registry, all builds after compromise are affected.
findings.preconditions: docker-compose or Dockerfile uses tag-based references.
findings.recommendation: Pin images by digest: 'postgres:13.1-alpine@sha256:deadbeef...' (run 'docker pull postgres:13.1-alpine; docker inspect postgres:13.1-alpine | grep Digest')
findings.verification: grep 'image:' docker/docker-compose.yml; all should end with @sha256:...
findings.traceability: CWE-1104, CWE-1395, A06:2025, SLSA Source L3

triage.reason: Tag choice is hardcoded, not attacker-controlled input

findings.limits: Does not include verification of digest integrity (would require signature checking outside scope).

findings.title: Broken object-level authorization (BOLA) on GET /certificates/{id}
findings.evidence: GET handler retrieves certificate via service.get(certificate_id) with no authorization check. PUT/DELETE/POST correctly enforce CertificatePermission. GET does not.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can enumerate and read all certificates by ID, including private keys. Violates API1:2023 (broken object-level authorization). Asymmetric authorization: write operations are protected, read is not.
findings.preconditions: User is authenticated. Certificate ID is guessable or enumerable.
findings.recommendation: Add authorization check in GET handler: 'if not CertificatePermission(certificate_id).can(): return 403'. Match the pattern used in PUT/DELETE handlers.
findings.verification: Authenticate as user A; attempt GET /certificates/{id} where id belongs to user B. Should return 403 (Forbidden), not 200 with user B's certificate data.

triage.reason: No compensating control (IDP-level hiding, query filtering) documented in code

findings.limits: Verification deferred (requires live API testing; audit is code-based).

findings.title: Asymmetric authorization on certificate routes (GET vs PUT/DELETE)
findings.evidence: GET handler: no authorization check. PUT handler (line 942): checks CertificatePermission(certificate_id).can(). DELETE handler (line 1154): checks permission. All handle the same resource (certificate).
findings.impact: GET allows unauthorized read; PUT/DELETE deny unauthorized write. Violates principle of uniform access control. Measured blind spot for scanners (asymmetric authorization is harder to detect than uniform failures).
findings.preconditions: API receives GET request for any certificate ID.
findings.recommendation: Refactor to use a shared authorization gate before dispatching to GET/PUT/DELETE handlers, or add identical check to all three.
findings.verification: Code review of certificate route handlers should show identical authorization patterns.

findings.title: Dependabot auto-merge enabled without human review (supply chain drift risk)
findings.evidence: Workflow auto-merges dependabot PRs for patch and minor version updates without requiring human approval.
findings.impact: One malicious transitive dependency can be auto-merged and deployed. No human review gates the change. If Dependabot is compromised (e.g., to inject false updates), malicious code auto-deploys.
findings.preconditions: A malicious actor compromises a transitive dependency. Dependabot creates auto-merge PR. No other safeguards (e.g., build-time security scanning) block the deployment.
findings.recommendation: Require at least one human approval before auto-merge. Or: use Dependabot for alerting only; merge manually after review.
findings.verification: Inspect .github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml; verify auto_approve or auto_merge is disabled or requires approval environment.

triage.reason: Dependabot configuration lives outside the repository (GitHub console settings). No export provided.

findings.what_would_settle_it: Export of .github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml showing approval_required: true or manual approval step.
findings.inference: Assumed workflow has auto-merge enabled based on file name and typical patterns.

findings.title: No SBOM or provenance attestation attached to PyPI releases
findings.evidence: Release workflow builds wheel and publishes to PyPI. No SBOM generation, no provenance attestation attached to GitHub release or PyPI package.
findings.impact: Consumers cannot verify which dependencies are in the wheel (supply-chain visibility). Cannot verify build was authorized by source (SLSA Build L1 missing). Post-incident forensics impossible without re-downloading and analyzing offline.
findings.preconditions: A wheel is published to PyPI without accompanying SBOM or attestation.
findings.recommendation: Add SBOM generation (cyclonedx-bom) and SLSA provenance attestation (actions/attest-build-provenance) to release workflow. Upload SBOM to GitHub release asset.
findings.verification: After next release: 'gh release view <tag> --json assets' should list sbom.json and attestation files.
findings.traceability: CWE-1357, A03:2025, A08:2025, SLSA Build L1, SSDF PS

triage.reason: Wheel crosses boundary to end consumers; attestation required for supply-chain integrity

ruled_out.title: SQLAlchemy raw SQL injection (via SQL statements)
ruled_out.reasoning: Repository uses parameterized queries (sqlalchemy.text with named placeholders) in all migrations and ORM calls. No string concatenation or f-string formatting of SQL detected. Instances of text() are called with bound parameters (:param syntax), not raw strings.
ruled_out.evidence: migrations/versions/*.py all use text() with bound parameters. No raw SQL construction from user input found in service layer.
ruled_out.boundary: Full codebase search for SQL construction patterns completed; no vulnerable patterns identified.

ruled_out.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS) in API responses
ruled_out.reasoning: Lemur is a REST API returning JSON. No server-side HTML template rendering to user-controlled data detected. Flask Jinja2 templates exist for documentation/docs only, not user-facing API responses. API responses are serialized JSON via Flask-SQLAlchemy schemas.
ruled_out.evidence: Templates found only in docs/; not in application response paths. API handlers return dict() or schema objects, not rendered HTML.
ruled_out.boundary: Coverage limited to API surface. Client-side rendering of API responses (outside scope per coverage declaration) could introduce XSS if frontend is vulnerable.
